extraction.name: POPE
extraction.description: A polling-based evaluation method that converts the evaluation of object hallucination into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No short questions about probing objects.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao and Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The evaluation dataset was constructed by randomly sampling 2,000 images, along with their object annotations and human-labeled captions, from the MSCOCO validation set. Polling questions were then generated by sampling objects using Random, Popular, and Adversarial strategies.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data consists of images, object annotations, and human-labeled captions from the MSCOCO dataset.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The visual instruction datasets (such as MSCOCO) suffer from an unbalanced object distribution where a few highly frequent objects dominate the dataset, causing models to disproportionately hallucinate these frequently appearing or co-occurring objects.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Synthetic visual instructions generated by LLMs can contain inherent hallucinations or unexpected descriptive information that does not match the actual image, which can mislead the models during training.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucinations in models trained on these datasets pose significant safety risks for real-world deployment, potentially causing systems like autonomous vehicles to make incorrect and dangerous decisions.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Datasets are used for pre-training vision and language encoders, fine-tuning models on image-text instructions, and evaluating/testing object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models.

name.evidence: we further design a polling-based query method called POPE for better evaluation of object hallucination.

description.evidence: The basic idea is to convert the evaluation of hallucination into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-Noshort questions about the probing objects ( e.g., Is there a car in the image?).

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: MSCOCO (Lin et al., 2014) is a large-scale image recognition, segmentation, and captioning dataset. Here, we randomly sample 2,000 images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions from its validation set

rai:dataBiases.evidence: As the visual instruction datasets of these LVLMs are mostly constructed based on MSCOCO (Lin et al., 2014), they generally share a similar unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Such synthetic visual instructions are generally longer and more informative, but may involve unexpected descriptive information (hallucination inherent from LLMs) that is inconsistent with the image, which could mislead LVLMs.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: The hallucination phenomenon hinders the safe use of LVLMs in real-world deployment, as it may result in unexpected consequences caused by these hallucinated objects (MacLeod et al., 2017). For example, due to an incorrect understanding of the extemal environment, an autonomous driving system would make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, which might lead to serious safety issues.
